title: Fewer things
hookLine: owning less, as the forest monks do
tomorrow: can wanting less turn into one more thing to want?

lines: DO I REALLY NEED ALL THIS?
cards: Moving boxes have a way of asking a question: do I really need all this? Mai's grandfather, Ông Thanh, is asking it this week. We met an old monk on the day about ageing well who got the opposite offer.
Today, look again, this time at what he owned. Mahakassapa was old, and he wore heavy robes stitched from cast-off rags.
The Buddha said to him, in paraphrase: Kassapa, you're old now, and those rag robes must weigh on you. Wear robes that householders give, accept their invitations to meals, and stay near me.
It was a kind offer from his teacher, and Kassapa said no.

teach.h: TWO REASONS: EASE NOW, AND LATER ONES.
teach.b: He told the Buddha why. For a long time he had lived in the forest, eaten only what came to his bowl, worn rag robes, kept just three robes. He saw two reasons to keep going.
It was a pleasant way to live, here and now. And he felt compassion for those who would come later: they might follow his example.
The Buddha said: good, good, Kassapa. Keep your rag robes. That's the teaching under fewer things.
Monks in the Buddha's order own little on purpose: robes, a bowl, a few needed things, and food that comes as a gift.

Kassapa kept the stricter forest practices, the dhutangas, and forest monks today still take some of them up, freely. Not to punish the body; the Buddha turned away from that road in his first teaching.
Fewer things means fewer things to guard, and an example for whoever is watching.

teach.h: THE WEEK: MUD, TREE, CRY, CUP.
teach.b: Now the week, gathered up. Sumedha took the long view, face down in the mud.
Bhaddiya, with nothing left to guard, cried what bliss. The Buddha was glad for Kondañña. Ikkyu handed back a broken cup.
Each one loosened a grip: on time, on a palace, on credit, on a cup.

how: Buddhist monks keep only a few requisites, such as robes and an alms bowl, and live on what is given; some forest monks also take up the dhutangas, stricter practices like wearing rag robes and living in the forest.

o: throwing out all you own to prove you're holy
a monk's rule against keeping any gifts at all
owning little on purpose, so there's less to guard

games.q: old Kassapa's choice — tap the pairs.
p: kept his rag robes in old age
ease now, an example for later
strict forest practices, taken up freely

s: the Buddha praised Kassapa for keeping his rag robes
'good, good, Kassapa': for his ease now and for those who'd follow.
owning less is about punishing the body
the Buddha turned away from harsh self-punishment; fewer things means fewer things to guard.
Buddhist monks must give up every possession, even a bowl
monks keep a few requisites: robes, a bowl, a few needed things.

games.q: your aunt is moving to a small apartment and gives you her good dishes, saying she wants less to look after. what fits Kassapa's story?
o: she's choosing ease now, and maybe passing something on.
she must be sad; talk her into keeping them all.
it's only about space; the dishes don't mean much.
games.why: Kassapa kept few things for two reasons: a pleasant life here and now, and compassion for those who'd come later.

practice: Pick up one thing within reach that you own: a pen, a mug, a book. Hold it and look at it the way Kassapa might, as something you need or something you guard. Then set it down, rest your hands empty in your lap, and sit.
Notice how little the hands need to hold for the next two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Fewer things: owning little on purpose, like Kassapa in his rag robes. For an easier life now, and for whoever comes after.

orig.note: Pali: the strict forest practices, like wearing rag robes, that Kassapa kept.

carryVoice: Your line: fewer things, and fewer things to guard. A week of keeping going, done.
